If a liver nodule > 1 cm is noted on ultrasound, follow-up imaging with helical CT or MRI should be performed. Repeat ultrasound in 3 months for smaller nodules detected on surveillance.B
Adopt an early multidisciplinary approach to management of patients with HCC involving a hepatologist, hepatopathologist, interventional radiologist, oncologist, and transplant surgeon. C

background.definition: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary tumor of the liver.

list.listitem: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the 5th most common cancer worldwide. Worldwide incidence varies widely with geographic location.
Age-adjusted incidence in the US between 1999 and 2001 was 3.3/100,000/year.
Between 1975 and 1998, HCC was the only malignancy in the US with an increase in incidence (80%). The incidence of all other malignancies declined.

In patients with hepatitis B or C cirrhosis, the annual incidence is 3% to 8% per year. It is 1.3% to 3.0% in patients with alcohol related cirrhosis, and is estimated to be 1% to 2% annually in patients with NASH cirrhosis.
Four cases per 100,000 persons in population.
Two percent of all malignancies.
The annual economic burden of HCC in the US was estimated to be $988 million in 1998.
Hospitalization charges in the US for HCC in 2000 were $509 million.
Between 1998 and 2000 alone, hospital charges associated with HCC increased by 40%.
Both incidence and mortality of HCC are higher in African Americans.
Ratio of affected males to females is 3:1 to 9:1.
HCC primarily develops in the setting of risk factors such as alcohol abuse, chronic viral hepatitis and certain metabolic and autoimmune conditions.
About 80% to 90% of cases occur in patients with liver cirrhosis; sporadic HCC in patients with no established risk factors accounts for fewer than 10% of cases.
A family history of liver cancer is an independent risk factor (OR 2.5); the combination of hepatitis and family history confers a large increase in risk (OR 72.5).

In a meta-analysis of 31 observational studies with 1.02 million individuals with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), smoking (+30%), alcohol use (+140%), obesity (+31%), diabetes (+108%), and hypertension (+42%) increased MASLD-related HCC risk. Dyslipidemia is associated with lower HCC risk (-22%) where as metformin (-18%), statins (-55%), and aspirin (-36%) may reduce MASLD-HCC risk.
See table for other risk factors.
The 3 main growth patterns are solitary mass, multifocal (nodular) and diffuse (multiple small scattered foci).
Vascular invasion (especially portal system) is much more common than biliary invasion.
Extrahepatic metastases are more common in patients without cirrhosis (up to 70%) than in those with cirrhosis (up to 30%). Common sites include lungs, regional lymph nodes, adrenal glands and bone.
Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with HCC are rare and include hypoglycemia, erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, and cutaneous manifestations (eg, pityriasis rotunda).
Surveillance is recommended for cirrhotic patients and certain hepatitis-B carriers with liver ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months ().B
Prevent neonatal transmission of HBV; check HBsAg in all pregnant women. A

A good quality observational study in patients with hepatitis B or C found significantly lower rates of hepatocellular carcinoma (NNT = 25) and liver related mortality (NNT = 14) in patients taking low dose aspirin. B

British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines (2024) recommend AFP and ultrasound every 6 months for patients with cirrhosis, as well as in high risk patients with chronic hepatitis B infection. Surveillance is not recommended for persons who are not candidates for therapy. See for patients with an indication for surveillance.

A large Danish cohort study found a 5-year risk of hepatocellular carcinoma of only 1% to 2%, and only 1.8% of deaths in alcoholic cirrhotics due to HCC. Thus, they found relatively little benefit in this group.

BSG guidelines recommend CT or MRI of liver if a lesion greater than 1 cm is detected on surveillance ultrasound or if AFP is more than 20 ng/mL (or consistently rising above patient's baseline). For patients with a lesion <= 1 cm detected on surveillance ultrasound, repeat ultrasound in 3 months. If > 1 cm evaluate as above with CT or MRI.
Cell-free DNA methylation markers are promising as a screening test in high risk patients but require further study in clinical trials.

A propensity score matched observational study identified Swedish patients with hepatitis B or C who either did or did not take low dose aspirin. They found a significantly lower rates of hepatocellular carcinoma (4.0% vs 8.3%, HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.62-0.76, NNT = 25) and liver related mortality (11.0% vs 17.9%, NNT = 14). There was a dose response effect seen, with longer duration of aspirin therapy associated with lower rates of HCC. Bleeding rates were similar.

Treatment of hepatitis B and C is recommended by British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines to reduce the risk of HCC. Treatment should be either instituted or continued following surgical or ablative therapy for HCC.

Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults age 18 to 59 years by the CDC and ACIP. Screening adults at increased risk is also recommended by the USPSTF. The combination of vaccination and screening is expected to ultimately reduce the burden of HCC in the population.
Prevent neonatal transmission of HBV; check HBsAg in all pregnant women.
Give HBIG to neonates of HBsAg-positive mothers within 12 hours of birth.
Initiate vaccination immediately after birth and complete full course.
Check for HBV seroconversion in children of HBsAg-positive mothers at 1 year of age.

Preliminary evidence suggests decreased incidence in patients with viral hepatitis treated with interferon and reduced recurrence rate in patients treated with interferons after resection or ablation of viral hepatitis-related HCC.
A large Taiwanese cohort study found that eradication of hepatitis C virus (e.g. achieving sustained virologic response) is associated with a lower risk of HCC.
The initial study for patients with a focal lesion on ultrasound is contrast enhanced CT or MRI if the lestion is > 1 cm; if < 1 cm ultrasound should be repeated in 3 months.B
Characteristic vascular pattern of a liver nodule on 2 differing imaging modalities (ultrasound, helical CT, MRI, or angiography) establishes the diagnosis for lesions more than 1 cm.B
Alternatively, characteristic vascular pattern on 1 imaging modality and serum AFP more than 200 ng/dL are diagnostic for lesions more than 2 cm. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Known extrahepatic malignancy, absence of cirrhosis
History of primary sclerosing cholangitis, evidence of cholestasis, elevated CA19-9
Absence of cirrhosis, characteristic radiographic findings
Mostly in women, normal serum AFP; consider contrast-enhanced CT
Absence of cirrhosis; mostly in premenopausal women in their 30s with history of OCP use
Absence of cirrhosis; mostly in women in their 30s and 40s; dynamic triphasic helical CT with and without contrast
Often associated with fever and chills; contiguous or hematogenous spread from another infectious process
Acute presentation with 1-2 weeks of fever and RUQ pain; history of travel to endemic areas

list.listitem: More than 1 cm nodule on ultrasound with typical vascular pattern on 2 coincident imaging techniques.
More than 2 cm nodule on ultrasound with serum AFP more than 200 ng/mL AND typical vascular pattern on 1 imaging technique.
Biopsy-proven HCC in nodules not meeting above criteria.

The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Staging System is recommended by BSG guidelines. It incorporates extent of spread, hepatic function, general patient health, and presence of symptoms. Stage 0 is very early, Stage A is early, Stage B is intermediate, Stage C is advanced, and State D is end-stage.
History and physical are of little value in diagnosing HCC at an early stage.
Large tumors may be palpable on physical examination; they may also cause jaundice, fatigue, unexplained weight loss, nausea, and abdominal pain.
Ultrasound is the initial diagnostic test of choice. A Cochrane review concluded that it is 72% sensitive and 94% specific (LR+ 12, LR- 0.29).

The initial study for patients with a focal lesion on ultrasound is contrast enhanced CT or MRI if the lestion is > 1 cm; if < 1 cm ultrasound should be repeated in 3 months according to British guidelines (2024).

AFP alone should not be used for screening unless ultrasound is not available or the patient's body habitus does not provide good quality imaging. The combination of AFP and ultrasound is endorsed by British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2024).

The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System categories predict the likelihood of HCC. A meta-analysis of 49 studies with 9620 patients found the following: LI-RADS 1: 0 malignancies, LR-2: 10%, LR-3: 48%, LR-4: 76%, LR-5: 96%.

A Cochrane review concluded that sensitivity of AFP was 60% and specificity 86% for HCC using a cutoff of 20 ng/ml (LR+ 4.3, LR- 0.47). Using a cutoff of 200 ng/ml, the sensitivity was 36% but specificity was 99% (LR+ 36, LR- 0.36).
An isoform of AFP, AFP-L3 was found to have only modest accuracy for diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma in a systematic review of 6 studies with 2447 patients (LR+ 4.5, LR- 0.71, AURC 0.76).
Lesions more than 1 cm should be evaluated by a second contrast-enhanced imaging technique (helical CT or MRI).

Given the accuracy of the noninvasive criteria for CT or MRI, biopsy for histologic confirmation is not mandatory. Tumor seeding is a potential risk associated with percutaneous liver biopsy and can have a major impact on prognosis.
If systemic chemotherapy with a biological agent is contemplated, the diagnosis should be confirmed histologically.

A risk score has been developed and externally validated to predict the likelihood of developing HCC in patients with hepatitis C infection. It uses age, treatment, AST, platelet count, sex, and presence of alcohol use disorder.

The ALBI risk score uses albumin and bilirubin levels to determine the prognosis for patients with HCC. It is calculated as ALBI = (log10[bilirubin] x 0.66) + (albumin x -0.085), where bilirubin is in umol/L and albumin is in g/L. <= -2.6: 18.5 to 85.6 months survival > -2.6 to <= -1.39: 5.3 to 46.5 months survival > -1.39: 2.3 to 15.5 months survival
See algorithm in for evaluation of the patient with cirrhosis and a hepatic nodule.

Hepatic resection or ablation and liver transplantation offer the best prognosis for carefully selected patients with early HCC. See for a summary of treatment recommendations by stage and performance status.B
Local ablative therapies are alternatives for poor surgical or OLT candidates. B
Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is recommended for large/multifocal HCC. B

Oral kinase inhibitors (cabozantinib, sorafenib) and monoclonal antibodies targetting PD-1 (atezolizumab) or vascular endothelial growth factor (bevacizumab) provide some survival benefit for unresectable HCC..B

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2024) suggest that adjuvant therapy with bevacizumab plus atezolizumab is the standard of care systemic therapy for patients with advanced stage HCC. Second line is sorafenib or lenvatinib. The same guidelines recommend against the combinations of cabozantinib and atezolizumab or lenvatinib and pembrolizumab. BSG guidelines describe the combination of durvalumab and tremelimumab as an alternative first-line combination.
Newer agents targeting tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis have shown promise in the treatment of advanced HCC.

The oral kinase inhibitor sorafenib has been approved by the FDA for unresectable HCC. A systematic review found that it increased survival by about 2 to 3 months in patients with HCC. The STORM trial concluded that hepatocytic pERK and microvascular invasion predicted poor recurrence free survival.

In patients with unresectable HCC, a randomized trial in 336 patients compared atezolizumab + bevacizumab with sorafenib. Overall survival at 12 month was higher in the combined therapy group (67% vs 55%, p < 0.05, NNT = 8).

The first indication of possible second line treatment option was the RESORCE trial, which showed an increase in median survival in a large placebo controlled RCT of regorafenib in patients progressing on sorafenib.

A study randomized 156 patients to transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) plus sorafenib versus TACE alone. Patients receiving combination therapy had a significant progression free survival benefit (25 vs 13 months, p = 0.006); overall survival was not reported. A meta-analysis of 5 cohort studies and 1 RCT comparing TACE + sorafenib with TACE alone found an overall survival benefit.

In a study of 707 patients with previously treated patients with advanced hepatocellular cancer, those randomized to cabozantinib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor) had longer median progression free survival than those randomized to placebo (5.2 vs 1.9 months, p <0.001). Moderate or worse adverse events were common, including palmar plantar erythrodysesthesia, hypertension, fatigue, and diarrhea.
See for a suggested approach to treatment.
Consider surgical resection for single lesions in noncirrhotic patients or patients with well preserved liver function, normal bilirubin and normal portal pressure.
Consider orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) for solitary tumor of 5 cm or less or up to 3 nodules less than 3 cm.
For early stage lesions (<2 cm), surgical resection is preferred over OLT due to long waiting periods for the latter.

Provide palliation with targeted ablative therapy for poor surgical candidates. The likelihood of adverse outcomes following surgery is higher in patients with a Barthel Index >= 85 points (72% vs 29%, p < 0.001).
A randomized trial found less blood loss and shorter procedure time for patients undergoing elective hepatectomy with stapler as opposed to LigaSure (tm).
Risk factors for complications during laparoscopic liver resection include neoadjuvant chemotherapy, lesion size and type, and history of previous open resection.
A systematic review identified 7 RCTs comparing liver resection with local ablation strategies, and found better recurrence free survival with liver resection (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62-0.92).

A network meta-analysis identified 37 RCTs with 3700 patients comparing different ablative and non-surgical therapies for small HCC (<= 3 cm). The authors concluded that percutaneous acid or ethanol injection are inferior to radiofrequency ablation, resection, and microwave ablation. However, the overall strength of evidence and quality of included studies was judged to be poor.

A Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials comparing local treatments and surgery identified 11 trials with 1819 participants. There was moderate quality evidence that hepatic resection is superior to radiofrequency ablation (RFA) regarding survival and RFA appears superior to percutaneous ethanol injection (PEI) or acetic acid injection (PAI). RFA is associated with fewer complications and shorter hospital stays than surgery.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 RCTs including 266 patients suggests that TACE (transarterial chemoembolisation) plus RFA gives the best overall survival results in early stage disease. TACE using drug eluting beads (debTACE) is similarly effective.

A systematic review found that major complications occurred in 5.3% of patients, with no deaths. Overall, complete tumor disappearance was reported in 10% of patients in cohort studies, and tumor regression in 75%.

TACE is recommended as first line noncurative therapy for large/multifocal HCC without vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. A systematic review of 11 trials and 100 patients also suggests that TACE with sorafenib may improve outcomes in unresectable HCC.
A prospective RCT using adjuvant radiotherapy after resection of central HCC with margins less than 1 cm shows that radiation is feasible and safe, and may offer increased progression free survival.
Another study found that in a small case series, stereotactic hypofractionated radiation therapy (SHORT) was useful as a bridge to transplantation.
The necrotic effect of RFA is more predictable and its efficacy is superior to that of PEI for lesions more than 2 cm.
Results from an RCT comparing TACE with Ytrrium 90 radioembolisation in 45 patients shows the promise of increased time to progression compared to TACE (>26 months vs 7 months, p = 0.001).
Patients with terminal HCC, poor performance status or massive tumor burden with markedly impaired liver function should receive symptomatic treatment.

For patients with HCC associated with hepatitis B or C infection, a systematic review concluded that adjuvant therapy with autologous cytokine-induced killer cells after attempted curative resection improved survival (RR 1.15, p = 0.02) at 3 years.

For patients with recurrence of HCC, hepatectomy and TACE appear to be similarly effective. Negative prognostic factors include having more than one metastasis, large metastasis, and a short disease-free interval.

Any patient suspected of having HCC should be referred to a center with multidisciplinary team consisting of a hepatologist, hepatopathologist, interventional radiologist, transplant surgeon and oncologist in order to stage the disease and explore all potential treatment options.
Patients with HCC should be hospitalized for decompensated cirrhosis, complications of surgery, unexplained fever and suspected intra-abdominal bleeding, or for surgical resection/OLT.
Patients with advanced stage HCC or portal invasion can be enrolled in ongoing clinical trials testing new agents.
HCC continues to have extremely poor prognosis with a mortality rate equaling the incidence rate. B
The 10-year survival following resection isonly 7%.B
Overall 1, 2, and 3 year survivals for nonsurgical HCC patients are 54%, 40%, and 28% respectively.

Prediction of survival in untreated HCC is inaccurate and complex due to the wide spectrum of presentation and degree of hepatic impairment. While several risk scores have been evaluated such as the MELD, Child-Pugh, MELD-NA and ALBI, all had an area under the ROC curve of 0.60 or lower.
Despite modern advances in medicine, the mortality/incidence ratio of HCC remains close to 1.
The 10-year survival following resection for HCC is about 7%, compared to an actuarial survival for a similar group of patients of 27%.
Local ablative therapies (RFA and PEI) confer a 4-year survival of 69%.

The ALBI risk score uses albumin and bilirubin levels to determine the prognosis for patients with HCC. It is calculated as ALBI = (log10bilirubin x 0.66) + (albumin x -0.085), where bilirubin is in umol/L and albumin is in g/L. <= -2.6: 18.5 to 85.6 months survival > -2.6 to <= -1.39: 5.3 to 46.5 months survival > -1.39: 2.3 to 15.5 months survival
The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer staging system has been endorsed by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and has the best predictive power for prognosis of HCC.
Factors which negatively impact recurrence following treatment include high-grade histology, number and size of lesions, and presence of vascular invasion.
The modified Glasgow Prognostic Score (mGPS) is an indicator of systemic inflammation and an independent marker of poor prognosis.
Pretransplant AFP >100 ng/ml and CRP >0.8 mg/dl predict HCC recurrence post-transplant. If both are present, likelihood of recurrence is 92% versus 2.3% if both are negative.
Order a CT or MRI of the liver every 3 to 4 months in patients with suspicious hepatic masses or markedly elevated AFP.
Obtain annual AFP, helical CT, or MRI in patients who have undergone curative treatment.
Patients who have received ablative therapy should get a helical CT and/or ultrasound as required.
Perform a clinical examination, AFP, and helical CT every 6 months for early tumor-detection in patients awaiting transplant.
All cirrhotic patients should be educated about HCC screening.
Inform patients with HCC about all possible therapeutic options including resection, transplant or local ablation depending on disease severity.
HCC in pregnancy is associated with an extremely high mortality rate.
Once HCC is diagnosed, focus should be on early termination of pregnancy followed, whenever possible, by surgical resection.
HCC is the second most common primary liver tumor in children (incidence = 0.29-0.45 per million children per year).
Best survival is achieved by complete surgical resection or OLT.

In children with hepatoblastoma treated with cisplatin, sodium thiosulfate was effective at protecting against cisplatin induced hearing loss (33% vs 63%, p <0.05, NNT = 3) and had not effect on survival.

feature.caption: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) Screening/Surveillance Recommendations by Patient Group.
feature.feature_body: Cirrhosis due to Hepatitis B, C, alcohol use, or NASH Hemochromatotis Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Advanced primary biliary cirrhosis (stage 4) Other groups with non-cirrhotic hepatitis B: Asian male carrers > 40 and females > 50 years; hepatitis B carrier with family history of HCC; African Black persons with hepatitis B, and patients with an elevated risk for HCC using a validated risk score. Data from Suddle, et al. British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of hepatocellular carcinoma in adults. Gut 2024; 73: 1235-68.

feature.caption: Treatment Recommendations for Patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
feature.feature_body:
Performance Status * and Childs Category Clinical Findings Treatment Options
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Single nodule <2 cm Resection, ablation
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Single nodule 2 to 5 cm Transplant, resection, ablation (if < 3 cm)
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Multifocal nodules and meeting criteria for transplant Transplant
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Single nodule 5 to 7 cm Transplant after observation, resection
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Single nodule > 7 cm Resection
PS < 2, Childs A, no MVI or EHS * Multifocal nodules not meeting criteria for transplant Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), systemic therapy
PS < 2, Childs A, MVI or EHS present Macrovascular tumor infiltration or extrahepatic disease spread present Systemic therapy
Childs B or C cirrhosis
If patient is a candidate, transplant. Otherwise active supportive with re-evaluation if patient recompensates or improves PS.
* PS, performance status: stage 0, fully active with no symptoms; stage 1, minor symptoms, able to do light activity; stage 2, capable of self-care but unable to work, up for more than 50% of waking hours; stage 3, limited self-care, confined to bed or chair more than 50% of waking hours; stage 4, completely disabled, confined to bed or chair. ** MVI = macrovascular tumor infiltration, EHS = extrahepatic disease spread. Data from Suddle, et al. British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of hepatocellular carcinoma in adults. Gut 2024; 73: 1235-68.
